1:
The sickness is read as a stroke with a purpose. Gill takes it for a disease sent of God in punishment of the father's sin, and admits the interval cannot be fixed. Clarke calls it a prelude to the miseries that fell on the house, and at the same time a merciful warning meant to turn the king from his idolatry. Henry presses the aim, since God had a controversy in hand and sinners must either bend or break, and notes that when sickness enters a household it is worth asking what sin is harboured there that the affliction was sent to convince us of. On the child Henry collects three things that did not shield him: rank, youth, and favour with heaven — all the kingdom mourned him, which suggests the heir-apparent — so that nobody should count on health continuing. Ellicott adds a curiosity, that the sons of Jeroboam and of Rehoboam bore the same name, which may be more than coincidence if both were born about the time Jeroboam stood well with Solomon.

What the king wanted to know draws comment of its own. Henry observes that the question was only whether the child would live, where it would have been wiser to ask what means might be used; he blames a notion of fatality that cut men off from means altogether, since if the patient would live they thought them needless and if he would die, useless — forgetting that duty is ours while events are God's, and that he who ordained the end ordained the means. His sharper point is that it would have been more pious to ask why God was contending with him, and to beg the prophet's prayers and cast away the idols, but most people would rather be told their fortune than their faults. Keil and Delitzsch explain the choice from the king's own history: he had slighted this man's earlier admonition and expected no favourable answer, yet it was he who had told him he would reign, and since that word came true he hoped for another revelation. Henry hears the same calculation and warns that men who disqualify themselves for comfort by sin and still expect their ministers to speak peace wrong both the ministers and themselves.

The disguise, the place and the present fill out the scene. Keil and Delitzsch explain that the prophet's eyes were set with age, the phrase used of the black cataract, so that natural recognition was impossible — which is why the Lord told him beforehand that she was coming and what to say. Henry makes the blindness an advantage, since the visions of the Almighty need no bodily eyes and are rather favoured by the want of them; and his irony on the disguise is the best stroke in his comment, that a man who credited the prophet with seeing through the thick darkness of the future expected him not to see through the slight veil of a changed dress. Ellicott supplies what Shiloh had become, a place barely mentioned after the time of Eli and the ruin that overtook it, where the old prophet still kept his office for Israel's good while denouncing the new idolatry; and the wife is to come disguised as a daughter of the people. On the present the three are agreed and particular. Gill thinks the ten loaves small enough for a woman to carry and probably of wheat, and reports that the cracknels, which the Greek version assigns to the prophet's children, take their Hebrew name from the points pricked in them for ornament. Clarke describes the same article as flat perforated cakes, the sort still called Jews' bread, used at the passover. Ellicott agrees the gift was designedly simple and rustic, and adds the risk, that an act of plain homage could easily degenerate into treating prophecy as merchandise.
4:
The journey and the reception are given in small touches. Gill credits the wife with two motives, obedience to her husband and affection for her child, and notes that the prophet could see neither her nor anyone else who came into his room. Ellicott explains the idiom for the eyes being set, the same word rendered dim elsewhere, and traces the metaphor to the solid opaque look of the iris under cataract. Gill allows either a dream or an impulse on the mind as the channel of the warning that came before she arrived. Keil and Delitzsch describe what that forewarning made possible: hearing the sound of her feet at the door, the prophet named her, charged her with the disguise, and told her he was entrusted with a hard saying. Clarke adds the motive for the disguise that the narrative leaves unsaid, since it would have been discreditable to the calves if it were known that their king had gone to consult a prophet of Jehovah.

The message opens by rehearsing what the king had been given. Keil and Delitzsch render the preamble as an exaltation from among the people and an appointment as prince over God's own people, against which is set a failure to be what David was, a doing of worse than all who went before — which one commentator they quote takes of the judges and leaders of Israel — the making of other gods against an express command, and the casting of God behind the back. On that last phrase they note that it occurs only here and in one prophet, and that it denotes the most scornful contempt, the strict opposite of keeping God before the eyes and in the heart; they also gloss the blunt idiom for every male and the paired expression for the fettered and the free. Henry fastens on the title God takes in the message, the Lord God of Israel, and draws from it that although Israel had forsaken God he had not cast them off nor given them a bill of divorce, and so would avenge on this king the greatest mischief done them, which was to debauch them and draw them from God. On the recital of favours Henry's comment is characteristically practical: whether we keep account of God's mercies or not, he does, and will set even the mercies in order before an ungrateful man to his greater confusion.

The comparison with David is the standard the king is measured against. Henry grants that David had faults, and some bad ones, but says he never forsook the worship of God nor grew loose or cold toward it, which is how he came by the character of following God with all his heart and was set as an example to all his successors — so that those did not do well who did not do like David. Against that Henry sets the charge of having done evil above all before him, and defends it by comparison: Saul, who was rejected, never worshipped idols, and Solomon did so only occasionally in his dotage and never made Israel to sin. He explains why the calves are called other gods although they were set up in honour of the God who brought Israel out of Egypt — because they were worshipped as the heathen worshipped theirs, because they changed the truth of God into a lie, and because many ignorant worshippers stopped at the image itself. His sharpest observation is that the richness of the metal was no recommendation, since gold calves provoked God under colour of pleasing him. On the rending of the kingdom from the house of David, Gill reckons the portion at ten parts out of twelve, and Clarke adds a necessary qualification, that God permitted the rending rather than performing it, the occasion being the folly and insolence of Rehoboam.
9:
The charge of having outdone every predecessor needs defending, and both commentators who take it up feel the difficulty. Gill defends it by comparison: worse than David, worse than Saul who never gave into idolatry, and worse even than Solomon, who connived at idolatry without attempting to draw the people into it — though he allows the clause may look only at those who had been kings of Israel before, and notes that if this was late in the reign, Rehoboam and Abijam may already have been dead. Ellicott states the objection more fully, since the days of the Judges furnish many instances of false worship, Solomon's apostasy was recent, and there were the golden calf in the wilderness and the old idolatrous sanctuaries at Ophrah and at Dan. His first answer is that the guilt was aggravated by contempt of a special promise given on the sole condition of obedience, which may be why this king above others is said to have cast God behind his back. His better answer is that the words look at the effect rather than the act: other idolatries came and passed away, while this one, planted at a critical moment, went on poisoning the springs of national faith and at all times made Israel to sin.

On the calves themselves Ellicott sets out the defence and refuses it. The king would have justified them as emblems of the true God; the prophet treats molten images expressly forbidden in the Law as being in fact objects of worship, which is what Ellicott says all experience shows such emblems eventually become. He adds that a later verse of the chapter shows the worship of the groves attaching itself to this idolatry, so that the emblem did not stay an emblem.

The sentence on the house is read for its tone as much as its content. Clarke disposes of the blunt Hebrew phrase in a line, that it means every male and should be so rendered wherever it occurs, and Ellicott hears in it a touch of contempt, that even the lowest should be destroyed. On the pair of terms that follows he is more careful: the original sets them in antithesis without a conjunction, as two opposite divisions of males, literally the one shut up or bound and the one left loose, which has been taken as the bond and the free, the married and the unmarried, or the child who keeps at home and the man who goes abroad — the last of which he prefers as fitting the context, like the old and young of other passages. The contempt runs on, he says, to the end of the verse, where the royal house is the filth polluting Israel and is to be swept away to its last relics. On the unburied dead Gill and Clarke agree in a line each, that the meaning is no burial at all and no place in the sepulchres of their fathers. Ellicott identifies the dogs as the half-wild scavengers of every Eastern city and the fowls as vultures and other birds of prey. He then raises the ancient belief that denying burial inflicted suffering on the departed soul, admits there is no means of knowing whether such ideas lingered among the Israelites, and observes that their law and ritual honoured the body in life as consecrated to God — which would teach that the body is part of the true man, and so deepen the repugnance with which reverent feeling regards an outrage on the dead.
12:
The one mercy in the message is the child's death, and the commentators dwell on it. Gill explains why all Israel would mourn, since the boy was heir apparent and a hopeful prince on whom expectations rested, that when he came to the throne matters would take a different turn in religion — so that his removal left them fearing things would grow worse instead of better. Clarke draws the general rule, that God will not destroy the righteous with the wicked and respects even a little good because it is a seed of his own, like the grain of mustard seed. Ellicott finds the declaration singularly pathetic, since an early death in peace and with due mourning is the only reward piety can be given when judgment is coming, and he compares the word spoken to Josiah before the fall of Judah.

Ellicott then steps back to ask how the Old Testament regards such a mercy. He observes that it gives little sign of the view that life is so burdensome that early death is Heaven's choicest blessing — the view Herodotus implies in his story of Cleobis and Bito — and that where something like it appears, in Job and in Ecclesiastes, the passages are clearly exceptional. His own summary is that life is treated throughout, sometimes even in contrast with the unseen world, as a place of God's favour which nothing but wilful sin can turn to sorrow; and that although the presence and penalty of sin are recognised from the Fall onward, they are seen as impairing and not destroying a natural heritage of joy.

The king to be raised up is named by both commentators who identify him. Gill says simply that Baasha is meant; Ellicott adds the irony that this instrument of judgment had a probation of his own, failed it, and drew the same doom on his own house. The closing words of the verse are another matter. Keil and Delitzsch supply the ellipsis to get the simplest sense — that God will raise up such a king this day, and then, but what do I say, he has raised him up even now — and note that the word order throws the emphasis onto the last phrase. Ellicott reports how far the renderings diverge: the Greek giving and what? even now, the Latin in this day and in this time, the Chaldee what is now and what besides shall be, with modern interpreters varying as widely. His own judgement is that the English version is not improbable and yields a simple and striking sense, in that day — but what say I? the judgment is even now at hand; and he sets beside it our Lord's saying about coming to send fire on the earth and what he would, if it were already kindled.
15:
The reed is read three ways, and the three are cumulative rather than rival. Gill takes it of political instability, the kingdom passing from family to family through civil wars so that there was continual disquiet and no settled peace. Keil and Delitzsch unpack the compressed Hebrew, that God will smite Israel in such a way that it sways to and fro like a reed in water under a strong wind, having no hold firm enough to resist the storm. Ellicott carries the same figure to its end, the reed shaken until it is rooted up, swept down the stream, and cast ashore at a distance — which is the exile itself.

That exile is the point of the threat, and it is the first of its kind. Keil and Delitzsch explain why it was added: not the king only but the people who had joined his idolatry needed to feel the severity of the judgment, so banishment beyond the Euphrates is announced, in the language Moses had used against transgressors of the law, and with the bitter turn that they would be scattered among the very heathen out of whom their forefather had been called. Ellicott notes that this is the first prophecy of captivity pronounced against the northern kingdom, and then enters a caution about all such utterances, citing the declaration in Jeremiah that if a nation turns from its evil God will repent of the evil he had thought to do. His conclusion is that a prophecy once uttered does not foreclose the probation of later ages, and that this is one more illustration of a truth we cannot comprehend but must hold, that God's foreknowledge does not take away the freedom and responsibility of man. Clarke adds the historical terminus instead, pointing to the destruction of the whole house and posterity of Jeroboam by Baasha.

The groves are not groves, and Ellicott's note is the longest in the chapter. The word is properly Asherah, the name of an idol, apparently a straight tree-stem surmounted by an emblem of the goddess it represented, from which he thinks the mistranslation entered our version through the Greek and Latin. It is taken for an image of a deity like Astarte, and Gesenius argued from the derivation that it was dedicated to her as goddess of good fortune; but Ellicott objects that the worship is far older than the introduction of the Tyrian Astarte and that the word is etymologically distinct from Ashtoreth. His most telling evidence is that Josiah is said not only to have destroyed the altar and high places at Bethel but to have burned the Asherah there, from which he concludes that the older worship, with all its superstitious and profligate accompaniments, grew up under the shadow of the newer idolatry. The moral he draws is the chapter's argument in miniature: from worshipping images as emblems to venerating the images themselves, and from that to worshipping many gods, the transition is unhappily only too easy. Keil and Delitzsch read the clause the same way, as a making of Asherah-idols, and on the verse that follows they keep the narrator's own account of the cause — that Israel was given up because of the sins of a king who sinned and made Israel to sin. Gill's note on the same verse is four words, that they were given into the hands of their enemies.
17:
The prophecy is fulfilled in two verses, and the commentators fill in the setting. Gill has the mother leave immediately on the word spoken and the child buried honourably, as his rank and pedigree required. Ellicott makes the incidental mention of the place do historical work: it appears the king had moved his residence, for a time or for good, to a town renowned for its beauty and lying further from the hostile frontier than Shechem, which seems to have remained the capital until Samaria was founded, and whose site is generally identified about nine miles north-east of Shechem in the high ground of Mount Ephraim.

The close of the reign is handled as a problem of what the historian chose to omit. Ellicott puts it most sharply: the exaltation and the promise, the idolatry and its punishment are all he cares to narrate, and everything else is folded into two phrases about how the king warred and how he reigned. He thinks the reign was probably prosperous enough in peace and war, the attempt on Judah excepted, and notes that scripture passes all of it over and remembers the man only as the son of Nebat who made Israel to sin. Gill supplies the wars that are known, with Rehoboam and then with his son, who proved more than a match. Clarke refers the reader to Chronicles for the important particulars. Gill reckons the twenty-two years against the neighbouring reigns, so that the king outlived Rehoboam by five years and saw the second year of his own grandson; Keil and Delitzsch add the succession of his son Nadab and observe that of the wars once described in the annals only the campaign against Abijam has left any account.

With Rehoboam the book changes gear, and Ellicott says so. From here on it is summary annals touching only the main points until the appearance of Elijah, filled out elsewhere by the Chronicles; and he characterises the first sixty years of the two kingdoms as incessantly hostile with the aggression on Israel's side — the invasion of Shishak probably instigated and perhaps assisted by Jeroboam, the attack on Abijah a direct attempt at subjugation, the same policy continued by Baasha and checked only by the desperate expedient of calling in Syria, until Judah even under Jehoshaphat was forced into something like dependence. Keil and Delitzsch date the new king's birth a year before Solomon's accession, and read the description of Jerusalem as the chosen city less as a rebuke to the ten tribes than as a contrast to this king's own idolatry; they also note that his mother is named twice without that implying, as one authority held, that she seduced him into it. Gill limits his kingdom to the two tribes of Judah and Benjamin. Henry finds nothing good to say of him and lists the five facts the chapter gives. He was born in David's last year and formed in the best days of Solomon, yet lived below those advantages, since Solomon's defection at the end did more to corrupt him than all the earlier wisdom and devotion had done to ground him. He reigned seventeen years in the city where God had put his name, with opportunity enough to know his duty had he had a heart for it. His mother was an Ammonitess, which Henry finds strange in a match David made for Solomon, guessing that Solomon was taken with her beauty — the name means as much — and that his father would not cross him, with consequences Henry turns into a warning about being unequally yoked with unbelievers. He had continual war with Jeroboam, and he died after only seventeen years, where the father, grandfather and grandson who reigned well reigned forty years apiece: sin, Henry observes, often shortens men's lives and comforts.
22:
The apostasy had a short reaction before it, and both of the fuller commentators reconstruct it from Chronicles. Keil and Delitzsch have the king brought to reflection by the prophet's word that the loss of the ten tribes was God's punishment for Solomon's idolatry, and following the law earnestly at first: fortifying cities, settling his many sons in them, naming his successor, while priests and Levites emigrating from the north strengthened his kingdom. Ellicott gives the same three years and the same causes — the judgment fallen on David's house, national feeling rallying round the Temple, the influx from Israel — and then the collapse, as the excitement passed and gave way to a reckless plunge into abominations of the worst kind. Ellicott notices who is blamed: not the king, as with Solomon and most others, but the people at large, this king being too weak to take the initiative in good or evil. His explanation of its depth is that the apostasy was the harvest of seed sown by Solomon's influence, under whose idolatry these young men grew up; and for the claim that it went beyond all their fathers had done, even in the darkest part of the age of the Judges, he offers the principle that sins committed in a more advanced state of knowledge are worse in guilt and subtlety than those of a semi-barbarous age.

The furniture of the new worship is described carefully. Keil and Delitzsch explain that the monuments were not images of gods but memorial stones, often commemorating a divine revelation, and like the high places were originally dedicated to Jehovah; the law forbade them nevertheless, partly as worship of human invention that easily degenerated, chiefly because the Canaanites set such monuments beside the altars of Baal, so that the two worships came to be unconsciously identified. Ellicott reaches the same conclusion by describing the objects, stone pillars on one side and wooden stumps on the other, perhaps each surmounted by some rude figure of the deity. He traces the pillar from the stone Jacob anointed at Bethel, through the commands to destroy such things as Canaanite work, to the ban on suffering either kind near the altar of the Lord. His point is that both might be innocent emblems of God's presence or images of false gods, the pillar sometimes linked with Baal and the stump with Ashtoreth, and that here the strength of the language shows the grosser sense — practised on every high hill and under every shady tree, which in those bare hills meant any tree notable for size and shade.

The last item is the one all four treat as the climax. Gill identifies the men by the vice named from the men of Sodom, records that one Jewish commentator takes the word of adultery and some versions of whoremongers, and observes that such practices commonly attended heathen idolatry in the temples and groves. Clarke's gloss is etymological: consecrated persons who had devoted themselves in practices of the greatest impurity to the service of the most impure idols. Keil and Delitzsch take the word as a collective covering both men and women attached to the shrines, note that the men had mutilated themselves in honour of the Canaanite goddess of nature, and identify them as Canaanites who entered Judah when idolatry gained the upper hand. Ellicott puts the horror in the derivation, since a word properly meaning consecrated here marks the licence and even the sanction of unnatural lusts in persons dedicated to nature-worship. Whether Canaanites or apostate Israelites, he reads their appearance as the point at which the corruption rivalled, and therefore exceeded, the abominations of the land's old inhabitants. His closing observation is careful: history shows plainly that such things are not incompatible with advance in knowledge and civilisation, but to find them sanctioned under cover of religious ritual marks a lower depth still.
25:
The invasion is dated and then documented. Gill fixes it two years after the apostasy just described. Keil and Delitzsch summarise the campaign from the fuller account in Chronicles: a powerful army, all the fortified cities taken, the capital reached, and the kingdom of Judah probably saved from extinction only because the king and the chiefs humbled themselves under the admonition of Shemaiah, so that the invader withdrew content with the treasures. They identify him as the first king of the twenty-second dynasty, known under other names in the Greek historians and on the monuments where Champollion first read it, and they point to the bas-relief he set on the outer wall of his pillar-hall at Karnak, where more than a hundred and thirty captive figures are led in cords. Ellicott treats the same inscription as the confirmation of the biblical record, since the names of cities traced in it lie partly in Judah and partly in Israel. On the northern names he reports a conjecture worth weighing: as an earlier Pharaoh took Gezer and gave it to Israel, so this army, coming as Jeroboam's allies, may have taken or helped him take the cities disloyal to him — and Ellicott thinks it not unlikely that the whole invasion was instigated by Jeroboam, out of the same desire to crush Judah that afterwards prompted his war with Abijam.

The spoil is itemised and its meaning weighed. Gill supposes the treasures were both the motive and the intelligence, since Jeroboam had made an intimacy with the Egyptian court during his exile and had no reason to spare a king who was no relation of Pharaoh's daughter; and he identifies the hoard as what David had left Solomon and dedicated for the temple. Clarke calls it the most immense booty ever acquired in one place and recalls that the golden shields were three hundred, all of beaten gold. Ellicott hears pathos in the phrase that he took away all, since treasures in which Solomon and Israel had gloried now served only to buy off an enemy. His more important observation is about what the verse does not say: there is no notice of a sack of the city, no desecration of the Temple, not even the stripping of its decorations, so that the record seems to imply the surrender of the city and its treasures rather than its storming. From that he draws a critical conclusion. The suggestion that this invasion destroyed all ancient monuments and archives, as the Gauls' capture of Rome is said to have done, has no support in this passage, and the conclusions about the dates of the scriptural records that have been built on it must go with it.

The replacement shields are a small detail that Keil and Delitzsch make informative. They note that the runners carried them whenever the king went up to the house of the Lord, from which it appears that he was accustomed to go to the temple in solemn state. They add a point about where the new shields were kept: not in the house of the forest of Lebanon, where the golden ones had been, but in the guard-chamber of the runners — a lesser treasury for a lesser article.
27:
The brass shields are read as both an economy and an emblem. Gill explains the plain necessity, that the Egyptian had stripped the king of gold until he could not replace what was taken. Ellicott grants the detail its accuracy and then its meaning, calling it perhaps a deliberate symbol of what had passed upon Judah, where only the semblance of the old glory was left and the fine gold had become brass. On the king's temple-going both are careful to give him his due. Gill observes that for all his idolatry he had not wholly forsaken the worship of God in the temple, and may have attended the more often for the late humbling providence; Ellicott makes the same point from the other side, that an idolatry like his father's would not have kept him away, while Chronicles implies that after the invasion he humbled himself and returned to the Lord. Clarke adds a calculation about the guard who carried the shields, that they were probably just three hundred, answering to the number of shields themselves.

The war between the two kings is asserted and nowhere described, which all three commentators notice. Keil and Delitzsch argue from the silence: since no open war is recorded, and the prophet Shemaiah had forbidden the attack the king was preparing against the tribes that fell away, the word can only denote the hostile feeling and attitude of the two rulers toward one another. Gill splits the difference by distinguishing an offensive war, which the prophet had forbidden, from a defensive one, which he thinks was maintained in border skirmishes though there were no pitched battles until the next reign. Ellicott is the most cautious. He notes that no such war is on record since the day the invasion was forbidden, and that no action by Israel in support of the Egyptian attack is even mentioned, though he thinks such action likely; the phrase may mean only a continued enmity that broke off peaceful relations, and with so little on record, certainty is not to be had. He adds, on the formula about the chronicles, that Chronicles assigns these acts to the book of Shemaiah the prophet and of Iddo the seer.

The closing verse gathers three small puzzles. Keil and Delitzsch treat the burial formula as the one used of Solomon, and explain the second mention of the queen-mother's name by supposing that it stood in that position in the sources the writer used. Gill reads the repetition as pointed rather than accidental, a reminder of what first led the king into idolatry and kept him in it. Clarke makes the same point with more force, that a man born of a heathen mother and begotten of an apostate father could hardly yield sweet water from so impure a fountain. His reflection on the succession is the sharpest thing in the chapter: righteousness cannot be propagated, being supernatural, while unrighteousness may, being the genuine offspring of nature — grace may be grafted on a crab stock, but nobody should do evil that good may come of it, since a bad stock yields bad fruit. On the son's name both commentators work. Keil and Delitzsch prefer the form used here as the older, explain it as father of the sea, and trace how it was shortened and then assimilated to a compound of the divine name, which is the form Chronicles always uses. Clarke reports the textual spread from Dr. Kennicott: the form here in five places, another in two, and a third in eleven others, which is also the form used in the gospel genealogy, the reading of thirteen manuscripts collated by Kennicott and De Rossi, of thirteen respectable editions of the Hebrew Bible, and of the Syriac.
